componentIdea.title: Stability and Instability in Physical Systems

chapterOverview.guidingQuestion: Why are some physical systems more stable than others?
chapterOverview.purpose: This component idea helps students learn to examine two aspects of physical systems—stability (stable vs. unstable) and state of change (changing vs. unchanging)—and to understand that knowledge of system conditions, forces, and energy impact predictions about the system.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: There are two independent classifications of physical systems—whether they are changing vs. unchanging and whether they are stable vs. unstable. Forces, energy flows, and initial conditions influence these states, while positive and negative feedback loops determine whether disturbances are damped, preserved, or amplified. Together, these interactions explain why some systems (e.g., planetary orbits) change predictably yet remain stable, whereas others move toward new equilibria or undergo runaway change.

K-2.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 2. Whether an object stays still or moves often depends on the effects of multiple pushes and pulls on it (e.g., multiple players trying to pull an object in different directions). It is useful to investigate what pushes and pulls keep something in place (e.g., a ball on a slope, a ladder leaning on a wall) as well as what makes something change or move. – NRC, 2012
K-2.progression:
At this level, students think of change only as motion. If an object moves, it changes, but if it stays still, it does not. They can experience change informally—a tower of blocks that keeps standing is “the same,” while one that topples shows change.

Teachers can help students notice that nothing happening can be interesting too, especially in places where motion seems likely. For example, tilting a smooth hardcover book lets a wooden block slide with a small angle, but a rubber eraser stays put until the tilt is much steeper. The difference invites questions like “What makes it move—or not move?” and creates an opportunity for student questions and student-led investigations.

A helpful rule of thumb for K–2 is that stable means hard to make move. A tower of ten heavy hardcover books is harder to topple than a tower of ten alphabet blocks.

Looking ahead, students in grades 3–5 will learn that systems can seem unchanging when changes happen very slowly, or that systems that appear to be changing may follow repeating patterns, such as a planet’s orbit or a swing’s back-and-forth motion. These ideas prepare them for later study of energy transfers, feedback loops, and prediction of change.

3-5.nrcQuote:
By the end of grade 5. A system can change as it moves in one direction (e.g., a ball rolling down a hill), shifts back and forth (e.g., a swinging pendulum), or goes through cyclical patterns (e.g., day and night). Examining how the forces on and within the system change as it moves can help to explain the system’s patterns of change.

A system can appear to be unchanging when processes within the system are occurring at opposite but equal rates (e.g., water behind a dam is at a constant height because water is flowing in at the same rate that water is flowing out). Changes can happen very quickly or very slowly and are sometimes hard to see (e.g., plant growth). Conditions and properties of the objects within a system affect how fast or slowly a process occurs (e.g., heat conduction rates). – NRC, 2012
3-5.progression:
Students enter grades 3–5 knowing that motion signals change and that there are explanations for changes that do happen as well as changes that don't happen—when things don't slide down inclines and when a sturdy tower shows stability by not toppling.

In grades 3–5 the spotlight shifts to systems that look the same yet are changing in slow or hidden ways. This is more nuanced than the earlier idea that any time something moves the system changes. Now students can look at a system where there is motion—such as a cup under a running faucet—and realize that aspects of the system are unchanging—the cup can only fill to a certain point. As it overflows, the cup will remain filled (unchanging) despite water flowing both into and out of the cup (changing). Students can begin to see how scale affects their ability to detect change. A shadow on the playground seems to be still over a minute but creeps across the ground when students compare photos taken an hour apart. Encourage learners to collect evidence over time—tally marks, timelapse photos, or graphs—so they can “see” the gradual change.

There are systems where the converse is true—the system appears to be changing, but just because some change is observable does not mean that everything is changing. For example, a pendulum swings back and forth yet repeats the same path; Earth spins daily while maintaining a steady orbit around the Sun. In the same way that evidence collected over time can reveal gradual change, these data can also reveal patterns of constancy within systems where change is obvious. Teachers can help students uncover patterns in data with questions such as What things are changing? What things can you find that are not changing?

Students will soon connect these hidden or patterned changes to energy transfers (e.g., heat flowing until temperatures balance) and feedback loops that either restore stability or drive further change. They will begin to analyze why a system stabilizes or keeps changing, not just whether it does.

6-8.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 8. A stable system is one in which any small change results in forces that return the system to its prior state (e.g., a weight hanging from a string). A system can be static but unstable (e.g., a pencil standing on end). A system can be changing but have a stable repeating cycle of changes; such observed regular patterns allow predictions about the system’s future (e.g., Earth orbiting the sun). Many systems, both natural and engineered, rely on feedback mechanisms to maintain stability, but they can function only within a limited range of conditions. With no energy inputs, a system starting out in an unstable state will continue to change until it reaches a stable configuration (e.g., sand in an hourglass). – NRC, 2012
6-8.progression:
By middle school, students understand that motion alone does not define change and that forces can cause or prevent change in systems. They know that change can be hidden when inputs and outputs to the system offset or when rates of change are slow. Students have learned to look within changing systems for patterns that remain unchanging.

Feedback mechanisms appear in concepts across middle grades, but there is not a unique standard within this component idea. Negative feedback loops pull a system back to some desired range—consider sweating and widening of blood vessels to lower body temperature or fill valves that allow toilet tanks to fill without overflowing. Positive feedback loops push a system away from the middle and towards the extremes or a runaway state. Students may have experienced this when a microphone picks up sound from a speaker and then amplifies the sound in a cycle that causes speakers to squeal.

Feedback loops are a conceptual steppingstone to understanding system stability. Previously students thought of stability as the system’s ability to resist change. This focused on the structure of the system—such as the relative stability of a stack of books compared to a stack of alphabet blocks. Feedback loops create a richer understanding of stability where change can happen, and the stability is the system’s ability to return to a previous state even after the change has happened.

The concept of energy becomes more nuanced in middle grades and students can consider how both forces and energy play a role in system stability and change. The natural tendency of all systems is to end up in the most stable arrangement. This explains why things will naturally fall downward, why salts dissolve, or why a compressed spring will jump back. In these examples, forces prevent the system from changing, but if the forces are not present, then the system will change towards a more stable arrangement.

A landscape of hills and valleys is a helpful analogy for understanding how forces and energy interact in systems. The system can be arranged in an unstable state (like a stretched spring) and this is like being at the top of a "hill." The spring will naturally pull itself inward to a more stable shape, which releases its stored energy. The valley represents this more stable arrangement of the spring.

Springs can be different from each other. Some springs require more force to stretch and therefore collapse more forcefully. The steepness of the slope between the hill and valley represents the differences between springs. A steeper slope represents the spring that is harder to stretch, and the additional force required to stretch the springs means that more energy transfers to the spring without stretching the spring over as great a distance. This is analogous to the way that climbing up a steeper hill takes more force to move up the hill but means that potential energy accumulates more quickly with each step.

In high school, students will explore more complicated systems and begin to see how the ability to predict the state of a system involves less certainty when there are more moving parts in the system.

table.unchanging: A system where objects do not move.
table.changing: A system where objects are moving.

table.unchanging: Systems may appear unchanging when inputs balance outputs or when the change is difficult to detect.
table.changing: Systems that are changing may have consistent patterns of change.

table.unchanging: Unchanging systems may not be stable; if disturbed, unstable systems will continue to change until they reach a more stable state.
table.changing: Changing systems can still be stable; stable systems use feedback mechanisms to return to a prior state if disturbed.

table.unchanging: Predicting whether or not a system will change depends on understanding the system’s internal and external forces and overall complexity.
table.changing: How a system might change and the accuracy of predictions depend on forces, initial conditions, and complexity.

progression.narrative: This component idea builds students’ evolving understanding of both change and stability in systems. In the earliest grades, students understand change only as objects moving or not moving; they learn that pushes and pulls can start motion or keep them from moving. By grades 3–5, students develop a more nuanced understanding of change, noting that seemingly unchanging systems can hide gradual patterns of change, especially when inputs and outputs balance or when changes occur too slowly to detect easily. In grades 6–8, energy becomes central to discussions of change. Students examine how energy transfers drive system changes and how feedback mechanisms can restore or maintain stability, or, in their absence, allow continued change toward a new equilibrium. In high school, the emphasis shifts to prediction. Students analyze how initial conditions, internal and external forces, and system complexity influence whether a system will change, the ways it might change, and how accurately those changes can be predicted.

standards.statement: Plan and carry out an investigation to demonstrate how pushing and/or pulling an object affects the motion of the object within a system.
standards.bigIdea:
Pushes and pulls can cause the motion of a system to change. Weak pushes or pulls can cause some objects to change shape, position, or arrangement, but other objects don’t change without a stronger push or pull.

*(Note: Advanced terms like net force or balanced and unbalanced forces do not align with the intent of this standard.)*
scientificIdeas: Pushes and pulls can cause changes to the motion of an object, including whether the object is moving or sitting still, speeding up, or slowing down.
Sometimes a push or pull is needed to keep a system from changing. For example, a toy car will roll down a ramp unless something is put in front of it to keep it from moving.
Things don’t move unless something pushes or pulls on them.
The size of the forces pushing or pulling on an object is important, such as a stronger push or pull will cause an object to move when it is opposed by a weaker push or pull.
A push or pull that might cause one system to move may not have any effect on another system.
Friction is a push or pull that objects experience from surfaces that they are touching. Rough surfaces help keep things from starting to move, smooth surfaces let objects move more easily.
The strength of the push or pull caused by friction depends on the characteristics of the surfaces that are touching.
Some objects can stretch or compress when they are pushed or pulled. They will return to their original shape once the push or pull ends.
studentIdeas: Things move because they want to.
Things move because they’re supposed to move once you let go.
If nothing is moving, then nothing is pushing or pulling on it.
Pushes and pulls only make things move; they don’t make them sit still.
Wind can make things go without a push.
Some objects decide whether to move. Big things are harder to move because they’re stubborn (not because they need a bigger push).
Things stop moving when there’s nothing pushing on them anymore.

standards.statement: Explain how forces can create patterns within a system (moving in one direction, shifting back and forth, or moving in cycles), and describe conditions that affect how fast or slowly these patterns occur.
standards.bigIdea: To figure out whether a system is staying the same or changing, you may need to watch the system and its parts over time.
scientificIdeas: A system may be unchanging even when it appears to be changing when inputs and outputs cancel each other out.
A system may be changing even when it appears to be unchanging when the changes to the system happen too slowly to notice.
A system may be changing even when it appears to be unchanging when the changes are too small to notice.
Even in a system that appears to be changing, there can be patterns that are visible over time.
Looking at a system at different scales may impact whether the system is viewed as changing or unchanging.

A ball rolling down a hill may appear to be unchanging because the ball continually rolls down the hill; however, measurements of the ball’s speed reveal that the motion changes as the ball continues to speed up. Examining further, students may see stability in the constant rate of change in the object’s motion.
The position of a student on a swing changes as they swing back and forth, but measuring the time required to complete one cycle reveals that the amount of time does not change.
The position of a planet in its orbit changes throughout the year; however, the amount of time needed to complete its cycle means the object will return to a prior position.
Forces can cause changes to the motion of an object.
When there is a pattern in the motion of an object, there will also be a pattern in the underlying forces causing the motion of the object to change.
studentIdeas: If the system looks the same, then no change is happening.
Changes to systems always happen at rates that we can see directly.
Changes in systems are always random and spontaneous (don’t look for patterns within changing systems).
